sigint:easy:sigint-e-20.prompt: A fictional exercise report came through a channel identified as compromised. Which analytical response fits the lesson's warning?
options: Accept the report automatically because security problems concern delivery rather than content
Publish the report more widely so additional circulation can establish its credibility
Conclude that every statement in the report must be deliberately false without assessment
Consider possible disinformation and reassess the report's support before relying on it

sigint:easy:sigint-e-21.prompt: A completed fictional assessment is ready for release within an authorized training exercise. Which recipient choice best matches the cycle's dissemination guidance?
options: Every participant who expresses curiosity about any signals-related classroom activity today
Anyone with a technical role regardless of whether the assessment supports their work
The authorized participants who need the assessment for the exercise decision
All recipients of the original packet even when their assigned exercise roles changed

sigint:easy:sigint-e-22.prompt: A learner proposes placing a fictional assessment on an unrestricted classroom display to speed delivery. Which revision best reflects the lesson?
options: Keep the open display because fast delivery establishes the required need to know
Use the authorized communication arrangement to reach the intended recipients promptly
Cancel dissemination permanently because secure intelligence communication prevents any sharing
Replace the assessment with every underlying detail so viewers can assess their own access

sigint:easy:sigint-e-23.prompt: Before reviewing a supplied fictional signals packet, a team argues over what its briefing should answer. Which cycle activity should resolve this first?
options: Dissemination, by circulating the unreviewed packet to every possible classroom recipient
Processing, by arranging the packet before identifying what the exercise decision requires
Collection, by adding material until a useful question becomes obvious
Requirements, by clarifying the information needed for the exercise mission

sigint:easy:sigint-e-24.prompt: In an authorized tabletop exercise, a student prepares supplied data for review. Another explains what the data means for the briefing. Which distinction is most useful?
options: Both are dissemination because the supplied data reached the class
Preparation guarantees accuracy while explanation concerns only the report's visual appearance
Preparation supports processing while interpretation for the briefing supports analysis
Both activities establish requirements because any work with information defines mission needs

sigint:easy:sigint-e-25.prompt: A fictional assessment reaches the intended planners, who identify a new unanswered question. What response best reflects the cycle shown in the lesson?
options: Return the new need to requirements and guide another appropriate review
Close the cycle because dissemination is its last listed activity
Reuse the same conclusion because new questions cannot affect completed assessments
Expand the recipient list until someone can infer an answer from the old briefing

sigint:medium:sigint-m-01.prompt: A fictional signals summary and a separate exercise report disagree about whether a coordination notice changed. The briefing question depends on that change. Which product best reflects the lesson's intelligence definition?
options: A transcript of the signals summary with the conflicting report placed in an appendix
An assessment integrating both reports and explaining the unresolved planning implication
A count of the documents received with the signals summary listed as the latest entry
A briefing adopting whichever report contains more technical detail about its original format

sigint:medium:sigint-m-02.prompt: After reading the lesson's objectives, a trainee claims that a fictional unit must already deliver fully reliable intelligence instantly. Which review comment is best supported?
options: The objectives express intended support and training goals without proving a unit's performance
The objectives establish reliability if a fictional unit uses the same intelligence vocabulary
The objectives prove delivery speed but leave the intelligence report's formatting unconfirmed
The objectives establish performance whenever the classroom scenario mentions secure communication

sigint:medium:sigint-m-03.prompt: An instructor emails a tentative fictional signals assessment and a volunteer's account of a public relief meeting. A student labels both confirmed SIGINT because they arrived by email. Which revision best corrects the review?
options: Classify both as COMINT from their email delivery and preserve the signals assessment's tentative wording
Classify each from its information basis but treat the supplied signals assessment as already confirmed
Classify both as ELINT from their electronic format and evaluate their planning relevance separately
Classify each by its information basis and retain the stated limitations on its claims

sigint:medium:sigint-m-04.prompt: A team submits a neatly organized fictional packet and calls it a finished intelligence product. It contains relevant material but no evaluation of what the material supports. What is the main gap?
options: The packet needs a broader recipient list before any intelligence work can occur
The packet needs more illustrations to establish the underlying claims as reliable
The packet needs evaluated meaning linked to the question the planners must answer
The packet needs an equipment section because every intelligence product concerns RDF

sigint:medium:sigint-m-05.prompt: A fictional written report describes noncommunication emissions, while a separate audio file contains spoken exercise messages. Both are supplied for review. Which classification is best justified?
options: The report concerns ELINT and the spoken messages concern COMINT by their underlying signals
The written report concerns COMINT because all readable reports contain communication material
The audio file concerns ELINT because sound recordings require electronic playback equipment
Both concern the same category because delivery formats decide the source classification

sigint:medium:sigint-m-06.prompt: A fictional voice message names a meeting organizer. The draft assessment says the organizer definitely spoke and was at the meeting location. What revision best fits the lesson?
options: Keep both conclusions because a name in voice content establishes identity and exact location
Remove the content entirely because voice messages cannot contribute information about people
Change the source category to ELINT because the identity and location claims are uncertain
Report the naming as content and qualify the identity and location inferences

sigint:medium:sigint-m-07.prompt: A student writes, 'The lesson covers COMINT and ELINT, so these are the only SIGINT categories that can exist anywhere.' Which edit preserves the supported learning point?
options: Replace SIGINT with intelligence so the statement covers all possible intelligence categories
Say these are the two SIGINT categories covered here without claiming universal completeness
Retain the statement because an introductory diagram necessarily lists every possible category
Delete ELINT from the statement because noncommunication signals cannot support intelligence

sigint:medium:sigint-m-08.prompt: A supplied fictional message states that exercise supplies have arrived, but a separate classroom record lists their status as unconfirmed. Which COMINT assessment is most defensible?
options: The message reports arrival while the underlying arrival claim remains subject to review
The message proves arrival because communications content always verifies the event it describes
The message must be reclassified as ELINT because a classroom record contradicts its content
The message has no analytical value because another record leaves the event unconfirmed

sigint:medium:sigint-m-09.prompt: A group points to 'Radio Receiver and Bearing Processor' on the equipment slide and claims the label proves its fictional direction estimate is correct. What should the reviewer say?
options: Accept the estimate because naming the processor independently establishes accuracy
Reject all directional information because component diagrams cannot contain useful labels
The label identifies a component but does not validate this particular estimate
The label establishes a sender's identity if the fictional packet also contains a name

sigint:medium:sigint-m-10.prompt: A fictional exercise packet includes an estimated direction and a communications assessment. A learner wants to replace the assessment with the estimate because it looks more precise. Which response is strongest?
options: Replace the assessment because numerical appearance makes directional information analytically complete
Use the estimate as a full transcript because direction finding establishes communications content
Discard the estimate because a direction cannot contribute to any intelligence assessment
Retain the estimate as an input and assess its relevance alongside the other information

sigint:medium:sigint-m-11.prompt: A classroom poster limits the lesson's broad direction-finding and advanced-analysis functions to spoken conversations alone. Which correction is supported by the function slide?
options: Describe the broad functions as relevant to communications and noncommunication signals
Expand the poster to claim every signal report establishes exact identity and location
Restrict the poster further to voice transcripts because technical analysis excludes other signals
Replace all analytical functions with equipment labels because a component list explains purpose

sigint:medium:sigint-m-12.prompt: A trainee correctly names the RDF components, then uses their picture as separate confirmation to remove 'estimated' from a fictional result before briefing. Which revision preserves both useful learning and sound reporting?
options: Keep the component labels and present the picture as confirmation because it depicts the relevant equipment
Keep the component labels and restore the estimate's qualification pending relevant supporting evidence
Remove the component labels but retain the confident result because component knowledge and accuracy are unrelated
Keep the component labels and move the removed qualification to a glossary rather than the result

sigint:medium:sigint-m-13.prompt: An older fictional report is well supported and clearly written, but a revised exercise question concerns a different issue. The deadline is approaching. What should reviewers do first with the report?
options: Treat its clear writing as evidence that it still answers the revised exercise question
Accept it unchanged because using an available report is always the most timely choice
Check which parts address the revised need before using it in the decision briefing
Reject all older material because age alone proves that its contents are inaccurate

sigint:medium:sigint-m-14.prompt: A fictional relief briefing is due soon. Some supplied information supports a useful limited finding, while one important point remains unresolved. Which response best combines the lesson's quality aims?
options: Deliver the supported finding in time and clearly identify the unresolved point
Delay all findings until every exercise uncertainty is resolved
Present the unresolved point as certain so the briefing will appear complete and useful
Send the full packet without analysis because the approaching deadline replaces evaluation

sigint:medium:sigint-m-15.prompt: Two fictional assessments answer the same requirement and arrive before the briefing. One uses elaborate technical language but weak support; the other explains a modest conclusion using clear supporting information. Which is preferable?
options: The elaborate assessment because technical vocabulary independently establishes report accuracy
Neither assessment because a modest conclusion can never satisfy a planning requirement
The elaborate assessment because more terminology makes further substantiation unnecessary
The modest assessment because its conclusion is better matched to its supporting evidence

sigint:medium:sigint-m-16.prompt: A fictional report's statements are well supported, but it arrives after the exercise decision and concerns a question the planners did not ask. Which evaluation is most precise?
options: Its supported statements establish that the report meets all three stated quality aims
Its evidence may support accuracy while its timing and relevance still reduce usefulness
Its late arrival proves the statements were inaccurate when the report was originally written
Its unrelated subject makes the original source category impossible to determine in principle

sigint:medium:sigint-m-17.prompt: A fictional signals summary and a separately prepared exercise account disagree. A reviewer proposes choosing the signals summary because its category sounds more technical. Which response best follows the lesson?
options: Choose the signals summary because technical source categories automatically outweigh other disciplines
Choose the other account because SIGINT limitations make every signals conclusion unreliable
Compare the evidence behind both accounts and preserve any unresolved conflict in the assessment
Merge the wording into one confident statement so the briefing contains no visible disagreement

sigint:medium:sigint-m-18.prompt: A fictional excerpt could refer to either of two classroom supply events. Direct clarification with the source is unavailable, and the interpretation would change the briefing. Which action is best?
options: Assign the excerpt to the event most convenient for completing the scheduled briefing
Remove the source limitation once two students agree on their preferred interpretation
Treat the earliest possible event as established because timing resolves all ambiguous wording
Explain both plausible readings and seek relevant support before selecting a firm interpretation

sigint:medium:sigint-m-19.prompt: A fictional report qualifies a notice change as uncertain. A copied slide deck repeats the change but drops that qualification, and a draft cites the two as agreement. Which revision best reflects their evidentiary support?
options: Restore the qualification and describe the report and copied deck as one underlying basis
Restore the qualification but keep the two documents as independent support for the change
Count one underlying basis but retain the deck's definite wording for a simpler briefing
Treat the omitted qualification as new evidence that the report's uncertainty has been resolved

sigint:medium:sigint-m-20.prompt: An exercise warning identifies a compromised information channel. One fictional report from that channel matches the planners' expectations. How should the team handle it?
options: Accept it without qualification because expected content cannot be deceptive in the exercise
Discard all related planning questions because a compromised channel prevents any useful assessment
Review its support with the compromise warning visible before assigning it decision weight
Increase its credibility because agreement with the planners' expectations removes source concerns

sigint:medium:sigint-m-21.prompt: A fictional assessment is relevant to a relief exercise decision. Its draft distribution includes several authorized classroom participants whose assigned work has no connection to that decision. Which revision fits the lesson?
options: Use assigned technical specialization as the recipient criterion where the participants hold the required exercise authorization
Match the recipient list to the participants who need this assessment for their assigned work
Use membership in the decision group's parent organization as the recipient criterion for this assessment
Use the existing protected mailing list as the recipient criterion because its membership has already been approved for exercise traffic

sigint:medium:sigint-m-22.prompt: The intended recipient of a fictional assessment changes before the deadline. The authorized communication arrangement can reach the replacement. What handoff best fits the lesson?
options: Use the authorized arrangement and confirm the replacement's need for this assessment
Post it openly so the replacement can obtain a copy without coordination
Use the former recipient automatically because the assessment was drafted before the change
Withhold it permanently because a change of recipient makes timely dissemination impossible

sigint:medium:sigint-m-23.prompt: In a fictional training workflow, the need is clear and the supplied material has been gathered and prepared. The team has not explained what it means. Which next step addresses the missing work?
options: Disseminate the material unchanged because preparation already establishes its intelligence significance
Redefine every requirement because information gathering makes earlier mission needs unusable
Repeat the gathering step solely to increase the amount of material in the classroom packet
Analyze the prepared material against the requirement before producing the assessment

sigint:medium:sigint-m-24.prompt: An instructor has already supplied all permitted fictional material for an exercise. A learner calls listing the packet's contents 'analysis.' Which correction best identifies the actual gap?
options: Listing contents completes dissemination because the packet already reached the training team
Listing contents establishes requirements because each listed document creates its own mission need
Listing records available material; analysis must explain what it supports about the question
Listing proves the packet complete because any supplied set contains all information the team needs

sigint:medium:sigint-m-25.prompt: Authorized planners receive a fictional assessment but explain that it answers an earlier version of their question. Which response best uses the cycle?
options: Resend the same assessment to additional recipients until someone finds the old answer useful
Use the feedback to refine the requirement and reassess what existing material can answer
Treat delivery as proof of completion because the assessment reached an authorized audience
Rename the analysis stage as dissemination so the old conclusion fits the revised question

sigint:hard:sigint-h-01.prompt: A fictional relief review has three inputs: a signals summary supporting a notice change, a copied briefing repeating it, and a separate account leaving the change uncertain. The decision is due soon. Which assessment best follows the lesson?
options: Treat the two matching documents as corroboration and qualify only the separate account
Present the separate account alone because acknowledged uncertainty makes it more reliable than any signals summary
Explain the shared origin, assess the separate account, and deliver a bounded finding before the decision
Combine all three statements into a definite conclusion because integration requires eliminating disagreement before dissemination

sigint:hard:sigint-h-02.prompt: A fictional course review claims that teaching secure intelligence communication proves both the students' assessments and a unit's capabilities are reliable. Which revision preserves what the lesson actually supports?
options: Describe completed technical instruction as evidence of assessment reliability, while treating the fictional unit's capabilities as a separate validation question
Describe secure delivery and consistent use of cycle terminology as the review evidence for reliable conclusions in the submitted assessments
Describe the students' orderly reporting and protected handling as evidence of both assessment quality and the represented unit's intelligence capability
Describe training and secure communication as objectives, then evaluate assessment quality from the actual evidence provided

sigint:hard:sigint-h-03.prompt: A classroom team has time to complete one final review before an authorized briefing. The packet is organized and securely deliverable, but its conclusion rests on an unexamined claim central to the decision. What deserves priority?
options: Evaluate the central claim and its limits so the briefing can explain what the evidence supports
Expand the evidence appendix before briefing so planners can evaluate the central claim themselves
Confirm delivery to the right recipients and defer the unexamined claim until their follow-up
Retain the packet's conclusion with a general caution that some information may be incomplete

sigint:hard:sigint-h-04.prompt: An instructor asks students to explain how supplied signals material could support a fictional planning question. A draft instead promises guaranteed answers and adds unsupported operational capability claims. Which revision best meets the assignment?
options: Keep the promises but remove the unit name so the capability claims become valid classroom analysis
Link supported information to the planning question and distinguish useful contributions from unresolved limitations
Retain capability claims as conclusions because the lesson's timely intelligence aim makes those claims self-validating
Replace the planning explanation with a component list because equipment names alone establish intelligence usefulness

sigint:hard:sigint-h-05.prompt: A fictional digital packet contains a transcript of exercise speech, a written assessment of noncommunication signals, and a cover email. The reviewer must classify the substantive inputs. Which approach is sound?
options: Classify the substantive inputs as COMINT because their written forms convey information
Classify everything as ELINT because the transcript and assessment exist as electronic files rather than physical events
Classify only the audio-derived transcript because a written assessment cannot preserve a noncommunication signal basis
Classify the transcript as COMINT and the noncommunication assessment as ELINT, apart from the packet's delivery

sigint:hard:sigint-h-06.prompt: Two supplied fictional messages use the same name and describe the same postponed meeting. The packet does not establish whether they share a speaker or source. Which assessment best separates the supported claims?
options: Report the repeated meeting statement while leaving common identity and independent confirmation unresolved
Treat the repeated name as proof of a common speaker and the two files as independent event confirmation
Treat the two files as independent identity checks because repeated message content removes the need for substantiation
Discard both messages because uncertain speaker identity prevents their stated meeting content from having analytical value

sigint:hard:sigint-h-07.prompt: An artificial packet includes only a noncommunication signal summary. One reviewer says it cannot be SIGINT without words; another says being ELINT makes its planning conclusion certain. Which response resolves both errors?
options: Treat the summary as raw data until communication content establishes its intelligence value
Agree with the second reviewer because noncommunication signals establish conclusions without the interpretive limitations of voice content
Recognize ELINT within the lesson's SIGINT coverage and still evaluate the evidence behind the planning conclusion
Reclassify the summary as COMINT once students discuss it so the claim becomes eligible for intelligence evaluation

sigint:hard:sigint-h-08.prompt: A fictional voice excerpt says, 'We are at the classroom annex.' The draft concludes that a named participant is there now and that the quoted statement was true. No separate support is supplied. Which edit is best?
options: Keep the location claim but qualify identity because the excerpt names no speaker
Keep the quoted content while qualifying the speaker, timing, and factual location claims as unconfirmed
Remove the quote because a communications excerpt cannot contribute any information without a confirmed participant identity
Convert the excerpt to ELINT because any unconfirmed location statement no longer has a communications source basis

sigint:hard:sigint-h-09.prompt: A fictional tabletop report contains an RDF estimate and an uncertain communications interpretation. The writer uses the estimate to label both the interpretation and the speaker identity as confirmed. What is the best review comment?
options: Retain the directional estimate but assess the interpretation and identity claims on their own supporting evidence
Use the estimate to strengthen the identity claim, while qualifying the uncertain interpretation
Omit the estimate until the communication's meaning is settled, then assess both together
Use the communication's apparent meaning to confirm the estimate, while leaving identity uncertain

sigint:hard:sigint-h-10.prompt: A classroom briefing presents one fictional direction estimate, the Doppler Antenna illustration, and the Receiver and Bearing Processor label as three agreeing sources. Which revision makes the evidence count defensible?
options: Count the estimate and equipment illustration separately because they present different supporting material
Count the two component references as stronger sources because equipment depictions are less ambiguous than fictional report wording
Identify the estimate as the report input and the equipment material as explanatory context without separate confirmation
Remove the estimate and use the component references alone because equipment context establishes the result's accuracy independently

sigint:hard:sigint-h-11.prompt: A draft function summary says RDF only handles voice messages and that advanced analysis guarantees exact conclusions. Which replacement best reflects the lesson without adding performance claims?
options: RDF concerns voice messages alone, while a component diagram establishes whether advanced analysis has produced exact conclusions
The lesson presents direction finding and analytical functions across communications and noncommunication signals without guaranteeing individual results
RDF concerns noncommunication signals alone, while advanced analysis replaces the need to evaluate uncertain communications information
The lesson presents component names as sufficient evidence that every direction estimate establishes an exact location and identity

sigint:hard:sigint-h-12.prompt: A training team accurately names both RDF components but cannot explain how its supplied directional information affects the fictional planning question. Its leader calls the briefing complete. Which response best identifies the remaining work?
options: The briefing is complete because recognizing both component names proves that the directional information answers the planning question
The team should replace the question with a component-identification task because equipment labels establish the only relevant learning outcome
The briefing needs additional equipment photographs so the existing conclusion acquires support from a larger number of illustrations
The team should evaluate the information's significance and limits rather than treating component recognition as a completed assessment

sigint:hard:sigint-h-13.prompt: A fictional assessment was accurate for yesterday's classroom question. Today's planners need a different answer before a near deadline, and only part of the existing assessment is relevant. Which response best balances the lesson's quality aims?
options: Reuse the supported relevant portion, state the remaining gap, and deliver it for the current decision
Send the earlier assessment on time with a note that the question has changed
Hold the relevant portion until the remaining gap is filled to preserve one complete answer
Update the conclusion for today's question while retaining yesterday's supporting analysis

sigint:hard:sigint-h-14.prompt: Two fictional products can reach authorized planners before the exercise decision. One answers the requirement with a qualified supported finding; the other offers a confident answer based on an unresolved ambiguity. Which choice is strongest?
options: Use the confident answer but add a general uncertainty note instead of identifying the unresolved meaning
Send both answers as equally supported alternatives and let the planners choose between their conclusions
Choose the supported qualified finding because timeliness and relevance do not erase the unresolved evidence problem
Delay the supported finding until the ambiguous product can be resolved into one complete briefing

sigint:hard:sigint-h-15.prompt: A fictional briefing already contains a supported answer to its main question. A late packet adds many technical details about an unrelated issue, and incorporating it would delay release past the meeting. What is the best response?
options: Incorporate the late packet before release so planners can judge whether its technical detail matters
Deliver the relevant supported assessment on time and assess the extra material against any actual requirement
Attach the late packet without review and keep the main finding unchanged to meet the deadline
Replace the main finding with a short notice that a more detailed packet is awaiting review

sigint:hard:sigint-h-16.prompt: A fictional report is delivered securely before the deadline and addresses the correct exercise question. A review then finds its key conclusion rests on a claim copied from one uncertain source. Which audit judgment is most precise?
options: Mark the report ready because timing and relevance are established, noting source uncertainty in an appendix
Retain the conclusion's confidence but seek separate support for the copied claim after the decision
Downgrade the report's relevance because the central uncertainty has not yet been resolved
Timing and relevance are strengths, but the conclusion's support still needs reassessment and visible qualification

sigint:hard:sigint-h-17.prompt: Two fictional reports agree on an event, but one paraphrases the other. A third independently prepared classroom record disagrees on a detail important to the requirement. Which assessment best reflects the limitation?
options: Treat the two agreeing reports as a majority that outweighs the third record without examining the origin of their claims
Recognize the dependent agreement, assess the separate record, and explain the unresolved detail's effect on the conclusion
Reject the separate record because disagreement with a signals report makes information from another discipline unsuitable for substantiation
Delete the disputed detail from the requirement so the existing agreement can be presented as complete confirmation for planners

sigint:hard:sigint-h-18.prompt: A fictional phrase could mean either that a relief discussion ended or that it was canceled. Source clarification is unavailable. Both readings support one minor finding, but only one supports the draft's main recommendation. What is best?
options: State the shared supported finding and qualify the recommendation pending relevant substantiation of the disputed meaning
Adopt the reading supporting the recommendation while noting that direct clarification was unavailable
Suppress the shared finding because uncertainty about the recommendation makes every part of the fictional excerpt equally unusable
Present both readings as simultaneous facts because including more possibilities makes the recommendation complete without further assessment

sigint:hard:sigint-h-19.prompt: A separate classroom record supports the time mentioned in a fictional communications excerpt but says nothing about the excerpt's speaker or the claimed event outcome. How should the assessment use that support?
options: Treat the timing agreement as confirmation of the excerpt's other claims as well
Ignore the record entirely because useful substantiation must confirm every detail of a communications excerpt in a single report
Use the timing agreement for that detail while keeping the identity and outcome claims separately qualified
Reclassify the excerpt as noncommunication information because a separate record has replaced the need to analyze its spoken content

sigint:hard:sigint-h-20.prompt: A fictional packet contains a report from a compromised channel and a separate exercise record supporting only one of its claims. A draft labels the entire report either 'confirmed' or 'false.' Which revision is best?
options: Treat the separately supported detail as sufficient confirmation of the whole report
Mark the entire report false because the possibility of disinformation establishes that none of its statements can be accurate
Remove the compromise warning because independent support for any detail makes security history irrelevant to the finished assessment
Retain the warning, distinguish the supported claim, and reassess the remaining claims on their own evidence

sigint:hard:sigint-h-21.prompt: A fictional assessment contains a useful qualified finding and a security-compromise warning. Its intended authorized planners need both for an imminent exercise decision; a wider classroom group is merely curious. Which handoff is best?
options: Deliver the finding with its warning to the planners who need it using the authorized arrangement
Send the finding promptly and keep the warning in the review file for later questions
Send the qualified assessment to the wider group to obtain feedback before informing the planners
Give planners only the compromise warning while postponing the useful finding until further substantiation

sigint:hard:sigint-h-22.prompt: A fictional exercise changes its planning question and recipient responsibilities at the same time. The previous distribution list includes people with no current need; the updated assessment is ready before the deadline. What should guide release?
options: Use the previous list because its earlier approval permanently establishes need for every later product in the same classroom exercise
Match the updated product and recipient list to the current need, then deliver through the authorized communication arrangement
Send the product to every participant because a changed question creates a need to know for anyone who attended the exercise
Delay release until the original responsibilities return because the cycle cannot support dissemination when recipients and questions both change

sigint:hard:sigint-h-23.prompt: A classroom workflow clarified the requirement, gathered the permitted fictional packet, prepared readable data, and securely sent it to authorized planners. The planners still cannot tell what the data implies. Which diagnosis best fits the five-stage cycle?
options: Requirements failed because any unanswered planning question proves that no mission need was ever identified at the beginning
Gather more material because additional data should resolve the planners' remaining interpretive gap
Analysis was not adequately completed even though preparation and an authorized delivery had already occurred
Dissemination alone failed because securely sending readable data automatically completes every earlier stage of the intelligence cycle

sigint:hard:sigint-h-24.prompt: After a fictional briefing, planners narrow the question. Some prepared data remains useful, but the earlier conclusion no longer answers the need. Which next pass through the cycle is most appropriate?
options: Refine the requirement, review reusable material against it, and analyze a conclusion for the narrowed question
Refine requirements and circulate prepared data, leaving planners to develop the revised interpretation
Preserve the earlier conclusion as the answer while noting that the question has narrowed
Begin a fresh packet before checking whether existing prepared material addresses the narrowed question

sigint:hard:sigint-h-25.prompt: A team has enough supplied fictional material to answer the current requirement. It proposes gathering additional classroom copies instead of resolving a conflict, then emailing the copies to a broad list before the deadline. Which revision best fits the cycle?
options: Increase the copy count and retain the broad list because more material and faster circulation establish a completed intelligence product
Resolve the conflict only after dissemination because sending material to more recipients automatically supplies the analysis needed for the requirement
Revise the requirement to fit the clearer report, then circulate that report before the deadline
Analyze the conflict against the requirement and deliver a qualified assessment promptly to the recipients who need it

elint:easy:elint-e-01.prompt: According to PAM 3-0702-01 as quoted in the lesson, what is ELINT?
options: A SIGINT sub-discipline dedicated to collecting and analysing voice and data messages
A SIGINT sub-discipline dedicated to collecting and analysing non-communication signals
An EW function dedicated to searching, intercepting and locating emitters for the commander
An EW function dedicated to attacking enemy radars so that friendly forces can operate

elint:easy:elint-e-02.prompt: Using PAM 3-0702-01, which pair names the two sub-disciplines of SIGINT?
options: ES and ELINT together
COMINT and EP together
EA and COMINT together
COMINT and ELINT

elint:easy:elint-e-03.prompt: An ES squad on the northern Luzon coast notes that the radar it has just located could be located in the same way by an enemy receiver. Which lesson idea does this reflect?
options: A radar must transmit to work, and every transmission can be found
A radar's weak echo is what an enemy receiver intercepts
Counter-battery radars are the main emitters that enemy receivers can find
A radar can be found by an enemy receiver once it has switched to tracking

elint:easy:elint-e-04.prompt: Which pairing of discipline and signal type matches the lesson?
options: ELINT: voice, text and data messages
COMINT: radars, beacons, sensors
ELINT: radars, beacons and sensors
COMINT: signals that carry no messages

elint:easy:elint-e-05.prompt: Which question is ELINT mainly meant to answer?
options: What does the enemy intend by this message?
Which friendly net is suffering mutual interference?
What equipment is it, where is it, and what is it doing?
How quickly must the commander act on this warning?

elint:easy:elint-e-06.prompt: At a Signal School exercise, an ES team and an ELINT team use the same type of receiver. According to the lesson, what separates their work?
options: Who tasked the collection and what the product is for
Which frequency band each team is allowed to search
Whether the collected emitter is friendly or adversary
Whether the collected signal is a radar or a radio

elint:easy:elint-e-07.prompt: Which three Electronic Orders of Battle are named in PAM 3-0702-01 as taught in this lesson?
options: Friendly, Adversary and Allied
Strategic, Operational and Tactical
Adversary, Neutral and Coalition
Friendly, Adversary and Neutral

elint:easy:elint-e-08.prompt: An ES squad logs a maritime-distress radio and an air traffic control radar near the northern Luzon coast. Which order of battle should hold them?
options: Adversary EOB, so that targeting is driven
Neutral EOB, so that civilians are not hit
Friendly EOB, so that mutual interference is prevented
Friendly EOB, so that OPSEC is protected

elint:easy:elint-e-09.category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
elint:easy:elint-e-09.prompt: In a Signal School waterfall exercise, one trace shows short hits spaced at exact, even intervals. Which source is most likely?
options: A rotating radar whose beam sweeps past once per rotation
A beacon or a radio that has been left switched on
People talking on push-to-talk radios
Data traffic made of many short wideband bursts

elint:easy:elint-e-10.category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
elint:easy:elint-e-10.prompt: In the lesson's radar sequence, what does the time between the outgoing pulse and its returning echo give the radar?
options: The bearing to the target
The size of the target
The range to the target
The carrier frequency of the target

elint:easy:elint-e-11.category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
elint:easy:elint-e-11.prompt: An ES team picks up a radar's pulses from a range at which that radar could not detect the team's post. Which principle explains this?
options: The two-way advantage: the receiver needs the echo as well
The one-way advantage: the receiver needs only the outbound trip
The echo advantage: the reflected pulse is stronger than the outbound one
The passive advantage: a receiving site is invisible to others

elint:easy:elint-e-12.prompt: Which radar fingerprint parameter describes the orientation of the wave?
options: Modulation and bandwidth
Beamwidth
Scan period
Polarization

elint:easy:elint-e-13.prompt: An ES operator measures a PRI of 1 ms on a new emitter. What is its PRF?
options: 1 MHz
100 Hz
10 kHz
1 kHz

elint:easy:elint-e-14.prompt: On the northern Luzon coast, an ES squad logs a new emitter at 9.41 GHz. Which NATO band does this carrier frequency place it in?
options: H-band (6–8 GHz)
I-band (8–10 GHz)

Withdraw all earlier findings before checking which conclusions the bulletin actually affects
Resend the original assessment with a new date because the issue concerns product dissemination

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-03.prompt: A briefing combines several reports from the same reported shelters but no data from others. Which conclusion best fits the evidence for a support review?
options: Assess the reported shelters and state that wider coverage remains an information gap
Extend the finding to all shelters because repeated reports create a sufficiently large dataset
Infer stable demand at the missing shelters because no reports describe an increase there
Withhold every observation until the team can establish a complete picture of all shelters

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-04.prompt: A short classroom review must explain a specific support gap. Most available files concern a broader background topic, and staff time is limited. What should direct effort?
options: Complete the large background review first because the file volume indicates a substantial need
Divide staff equally among topics so all available folders receive consistent review effort
Prioritize the specific decision requirement and the information gaps that affect answering it
Use the background files to draft a recommendation and define the requirement after briefing

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-05.prompt: The leader asks for 'current shelter needs,' but staff disagree whether the decision concerns present demand or likely changes. What should happen before the review expands?
options: Clarify the intended decision with the leader and adjust the information requirements accordingly
Produce two complete assessments before asking the leader which interpretation meets the need
Use the interpretation supported by existing slides and record the alternative in an appendix
Collect all available reports first and let the resulting material determine the briefing question

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-06.prompt: A tabletop storm update changes the support concern, but the team has nearly finished an earlier review. Which direction best balances completed work and the changed need?
options: Finish the earlier review in full before checking how it relates to the changed support concern
Discard the earlier review and recreate every dataset before evaluating the new requirements
Keep the original priorities and ask the audience to infer the effects of the changed concern
Reassess priorities and retain completed work that still helps answer the changed decision need

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-07.prompt: Reviewers discover that a draft cannot answer whether the exercise support gap is changing over time. Which follow-up direction is most useful?
options: Request more files across subjects so the larger dataset gives the analyst additional context
Redesign the dashboard so the existing snapshot communicates the possible demand change clearly
Specify the missing time comparison that the analyst needs to answer the decision question
Request a firmer recommendation so the product can answer the question with greater confidence

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-08.prompt: A student classifies a public disaster bulletin as COMINT because it arrived by email, while classifying a recorded authorized interview as ELINT. Which review is best?
options: Keep both labels because the delivery network and recording equipment define the source type
Classify the public bulletin as OSINT and the human source's authorized account as HUMINT
Classify both as SIGINT because each source became electronic material before staff review
Classify both as IMINT because a display can show the material as text or other visual content

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-09.prompt: A classroom packet contains translated simulated communications and a sorted table of noncommunication radar emissions. Both are displayed as charts, but neither has been assessed. Which review note correctly addresses source category and stage?
options: Retain COMINT and ELINT under SIGINT; translation and sorting prepare inputs, but assessment remains
Retain COMINT and ELINT under SIGINT; their translated and sorted form completes analysis and production
Reclassify both as IMINT because they appear in charts; retain analysis as the next unfinished task
Reclassify both as ELINT because they are electronic; translation and sorting complete their assessment

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-10.prompt: An abstract exercise describes repeated monitoring for change, capture of a transmitted signal, and evaluation of its significance as three separate activities. Which review preserves their distinctions?
options: Use interception for all three activities because each can occur before a final product is written
Use production for monitoring, collection for capture and dissemination for significance review
Use surveillance for monitoring, interception for capture and signal analysis for significance review
Use surveillance for all three activities because monitoring provides context for later understanding

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-11.prompt: A training image and a public bulletin describe the same shelter issue differently. What does the presence of two collection disciplines establish by itself?
options: Prefer the training image because the visible source provides a firmer basis than a written bulletin
Prefer the public bulletin because publication gives its stated figures a stronger status than imagery
Treat the two disciplines as mutual validation because their different source types reduce uncertainty
Recognize different collection inputs and analyze the disagreement before selecting a supported finding

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-12.prompt: A team translates reports, standardizes their dates and notices an apparent rise in demand. Which handoff most clearly separates preparation from assessment?
options: Hand usable material and the observed pattern to analysis without treating its meaning as settled
Record the rise as an established finding because the reports now use consistent dates and language
Send only the final chart to analysis because preparation has already resolved the source context
Return all material to collection because a pattern cannot be recorded during the processing stage

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-13.prompt: Two fictional reports use the word 'capacity' differently. Their figures look contradictory after sorting. What preparation best supports a meaningful later comparison?
options: Average the two figures so the analyst receives a single value that is easier to interpret
Clarify what each capacity figure describes before deciding whether the numbers can be compared
Use the larger figure so the briefing accounts for the greater apparent support requirement
Use identical wording for both headings so the figures can enter the same comparison table

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-14.prompt: An authorized classroom decoding demonstration succeeds, but the readable message is incomplete and its significance unclear. Which status should accompany it?
options: Label it a completed assessment because successful access supplies the basis for accepting its content
Label it a final recommendation because the accessible content can now be presented to the leader
Label it an invalid source because processing failed to produce a complete analytical conclusion
Label it a usable but incomplete input whose meaning still needs interpretation before assessment

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-15.prompt: The leader asks both how shelter demand changed over several days and how it relates to supply requests. Which analytical plan best fits both questions?
options: Sort once by sender and use that arrangement to explain both the change and the relationship
Compare only the latest totals so differences in reporting days do not complicate the briefing
Use trend analysis for change over time and correlation for the relationship between the measures
Chart each file separately so the briefing can present both subjects without further interpretation

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-16.prompt: A draft calls demand 'steadily rising,' but one day covers fewer shelters than the others. What review response best addresses the conclusion?
options: Check whether the observations are comparable and qualify the trend if the coverage gap affects it
Accept the wording because placing the totals in date order establishes a meaningful time trend
Replace the incomplete day's total with the highest value to represent the possible missing demand
Retain the wording but remove the dates so the coverage difference does not distract the audience

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-17.prompt: Shelter demand and supply requests rose together in the exercise dataset. A draft says demand caused every request increase. Which revision best supports a decision?
options: Retain the causal explanation but place its supporting comparison in the appendix for later review
Omit the relationship because correlation cannot provide useful understanding without proof of cause
Replace the explanation with a recommendation so the briefing can focus on the decision required
Report the observed relationship while explaining that this comparison has not established its cause

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-18.prompt: An artificial signal-label dataset contains recurring shapes across entries but no time sequence. The draft calls this a time trend. Which correction best fits the available data?
options: Keep the trend label because recurrence across entries demonstrates change across successive periods
Describe recurring characteristics as a pattern without claiming that they establish change over time
Assign dates from the order of entries and use that sequence to analyze a possible time trend
Discard the dataset because an artificial source cannot support the lesson's pattern-analysis distinction

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-19.prompt: A short tabletop briefing must recommend further review of a support issue despite an unresolved report conflict. Which structure best supports an informed decision?
options: Present the recommendation with the archive, allowing recipients to reconstruct the supporting analysis
Present the conflicting totals alone so the audience can choose a recommendation during discussion
Present supported findings, explain how the conflict limits them and connect a recommendation to that analysis
Present the strongest conclusion without the conflict so the short briefing gives a clear direction

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-20.prompt: A revised assessment changes a support assumption, but the current dashboard and planning summary still show the old one. Which response best integrates the update?
options: Update the affected displays and review planning assumptions in light of the revised assessment
Send the revised file and treat a delivery notification as evidence that the plan has changed
Update the dashboard's date but keep the old conclusion to preserve consistency across displays
Archive the revision and leave the planning summary until users request a review of the change

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-21.prompt: An authorized leader needs a short assessment before a discussion. One relevant issue remains uncertain, but supported findings are available. Which delivery best serves the stated need?
options: Wait until the uncertainty disappears even if the assessment arrives after the decision discussion
Deliver supported findings before the discussion and make the unresolved issue clear to the leader
Deliver only raw files before the discussion because an unresolved issue prevents useful assessment
Deliver a firm conclusion before the discussion and omit the unresolved issue from the brief

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-22.prompt: A clear chart reaches authorized staff, but its caption drops the assessment's limited coverage and staff use it for a wider planning assumption. What correction matters most?
options: Increase the chart's resolution so staff can read the same finding more clearly during planning
Send the chart to more staff so a broader audience can consider the planning assumption it supports
Restore the coverage limitation and review the wider assumption that relied on the incomplete caption
Change the chart's colors and retain the assumption because delivery reached authorized staff members

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-23.prompt: An unexpected account requests the full exercise assessment through a familiar-looking message, citing urgency. What response best combines decision support with OPSEC?
options: Verify the requester's authorization and use the approved route for any assessment sharing permitted
Send the assessment because the message's familiar appearance provides sufficient evidence of authorization
Remove the title and send the content so the recipient can meet the urgent stated information need
Forward the product to a broader group so another participant can decide whether the request is valid

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-24.prompt: An assessment's reasoning is useful for a public exercise summary, but its source appendix contains unnecessary civilian identifiers. Which handling best fits the lesson?
options: Release the complete appendix because explaining the reasoning requires publishing every underlying detail
Prepare a permitted summary that explains the findings without disclosing unnecessary civilian identifiers
Withhold the entire summary because the source material contains some details about individual civilians
Share the appendix informally so a useful explanation can reach readers without a formal release step

intcycle:hard:intcycle-h-25.prompt: A partner in a disaster tabletop needs a general finding, while the detailed assessment has access restrictions. What is the best basis for sharing?
options: Use the partner's exercise-liaison role as the release basis and send the relevant extract through the usual protected channel
Use a brief summary's reduced detail as the release basis and route it through the team's approved internal distribution list
Use the partner's existing system access as the release basis and provide the findings needed for the coordination task
Confirm what the partner may receive and provide a useful summary through an authorized sharing route
